objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain when and why a pilot makes an emergency descent, fly it from the right seat inside the AFH airspeed limits while you narrate it, and brief, supervise and debrief a learner's emergency descent so that the errors are caught early and the practice itself stays safe.
why: An emergency descent is the maneuver for getting down as fast as possible, to a lower altitude or to the ground, after a fire, a loss of pressurization or anything else that demands it [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. Learners rarely see one for real, so the habits they build with you are the ones they will use. Many responses under threat are automatic, which is why proper training in emergency operations has to come before the real emergency [[25:48|AIH 2-15]].

prereading.what: Emergency descents: purpose, the turn, bank, configuration, airspeed limits, recovery and engine cooling; then engine, electrical and cabin fires and smoke.
prereading.label: AFH 18-8 to 18-10

prereading.what: VLE and VLO, why gear speeds exist, and the placard where you find them.
prereading.label: AFH 12-16

prereading.what: Airspeed indicator markings and the limits that are not on the dial (VA, VLO, VLE).
prereading.label: PHAK 8-9 to 8-10

prereading.what: VA and its limits, load factor in pull-ups and push-overs, rough air, and limit loads.
prereading.label: PHAK 5-35 to 5-37

prereading.what: Coriolis illusion and the graveyard spiral; leading a level-off by 10 percent of the descent rate.
prereading.label: IFH 3-6, 7-50

prereading.what: Instructor risk management: crowded practice airspace, teaching at the wrong time or altitude, and prompting the learner to name hazards.
prereading.label: AIH 10-7 to 10-8

prereading.what: Situational awareness, time management, declaring an emergency, and SRM: prioritize tasks and manage workload in an emergency.
prereading.label: RMH 6-4, 8-3

warmup: Think first: your private pilot learner is flying a complex single at 8,500 ft. You say 'Simulated: smoke in the cabin, get us down.' They pull the throttle, shove the nose over, drop the gear and the flaps, and watch the airspeed climb toward the white arc's top while staring at the panel. Name three things that just went wrong. Which one would you fix first, from the right seat, in the next five seconds? And what should you have said on the ground so that none of it happened?

key_terms.def: A maneuver for descending as rapidly as possible to a lower altitude or to the ground for an emergency landing, without exceeding any structural limitation [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

Lift pressing the occupants into their seats. The AFH bank of about 30 to 45 degrees is set to keep it positive [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]; a sharp push-over can take it toward zero or negative [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]].
Never-exceed speed, the red line. Operating above it is prohibited since it may cause damage or structural failure [[24:389|AFH G-17]].
Maximum structural cruising speed, the top of the green arc. Do not exceed it except in smooth air [[24:389|AFH G-17]].
The maximum speed with the flaps extended; the upper limit of the white arc [[24:389|AFH G-17]].
The maximum speed at which the flaps can be extended or retracted [[24:389|AFH G-17]].
Landing gear operating speed: the maximum speed at which the gear may be operated through its cycle [[24:247|AFH 12-16]].
Landing gear extended speed: the maximum speed at which the airplane can be flown with the gear extended [[24:247|AFH 12-16]].
Design maneuvering speed: the rough-air speed and the maximum speed for abrupt maneuvers; it changes with weight [[24:389|AFH G-17]].
Pulling out of a dive while rolling. The design limit is exceeded more easily this way, so unload and roll level first [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].
After a long turn, a head movement in a different plane can create the illusion of turning on another axis [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].
A premeditated landing, on or off an airport, when further flight is possible but inadvisable [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].

chunks.title: What this Task asks of an instructor

body.p: The purpose in one line: descend the airplane as soon and as rapidly as possible while not exceeding any structural limitations [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. The destination is either a lower altitude or the ground for an emergency landing [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. Everything you teach in this lesson hangs on the two halves of that sentence: fast, and inside the limits.

The procedure in outline: simulated emergency descents are made in a turn, to check for traffic below and to look for a possible emergency landing area; a radio call announcing the descent may be appropriate; and the bank on entry is about 30 to 45 degrees to keep the load factor positive [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. Configuration and airspeeds come from the manufacturer [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

head: CFI ACS element
What changes for you
rows: K1 Purpose of and procedures for emergency descent
You explain the why, not only the steps (CFI ACS AI.XII.A.K1)
K6 and S7 Common errors
You name the errors a learner makes and analyze and correct them, often with the evaluator playing the learner (CFI ACS AI.XII.A.K6, S7)
S4 Bank
"Use bank angle between 30° and 45° to maintain positive load factors during the descent" (CFI ACS AI.XII.A.S4)
S5 Airspeed and level-off
"Maintain appropriate airspeed +0/-10 knots, and level off at a specified altitude ±100 feet" (CFI ACS AI.XII.A.S5)

body.p: Compared with the Commercial ACS: the bank, airspeed and level-off lines are word for word the same (Commercial ACS CA.IX.A.S4, S5; CFI ACS AI.XII.A.S4, S5). The CFI Task adds K1 purpose and procedures, K6 common errors and S7 analyze and correct common errors, where the commercial S7 was SRM (Commercial ACS CA.IX.A.S7). Your flying must still be at commercial standard while you talk.

Where the background lives: the Private (PA.IX.A) and Commercial (CA.IX.A) lessons cover decompression and time of useful consciousness, the Vg diagram, fire types and distress calls in depth. This lesson uses them and stays on the instructor's side: when and why, how to brief and demonstrate it safely, and how to spot and fix errors.

callout.text: Manufacturer first. The AFH emergency guidance is generic and does not replace the AFM/POH; if they conflict, the manufacturer's procedures take precedence [[24:350|AFH 18-1]]. Emergency descent training should be performed as the manufacturer recommends, including configuration and airspeeds [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

check.q: State the AFH objective of the emergency descent in one sentence, and say which part of it limits how fast you may go.
check.a: Descend as soon and as rapidly as possible while not exceeding any structural limitations of the airplane [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. The structural limits part sets the speed ceiling.

chunks.title: When and why: depressurization, smoke and engine fire

body.p: The AFH names an uncontrollable fire, a sudden loss of cabin pressurization, or any other situation demanding an immediate and rapid descent [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. The ACS gives three examples by name: depressurization, smoke and engine fire (CFI ACS AI.XII.A.K2). Teach each one with its own reason, because the reason decides how fast you go and how you configure.

head: Situation
Why get down
What it changes in the descent
rows: Depressurization

The primary danger is hypoxia; quick, proper use of oxygen equipment is needed to avoid unconsciousness. Evolved gas decompression sickness and, with structural damage, being blown out near an opening are the other dangers [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]
Oxygen first, then a rapid descent from altitude, which is necessary to minimize these problems [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]. In the ASEL world this is the pressurized single
Smoke (unpressurized)
Severe smoke harms everyone aboard; passengers and crew should use oxygen masks if available and the pilot should start an immediate descent [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]
On some airplanes, lowering the gear and/or flaps can aggravate a cabin smoke problem [[24:359|AFH 18-10]], so the POH smoke procedure decides the configuration
Smoke (pressurized)
Pressurization air normally removes smoke, but not intense smoke [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]
Depressurize at altitude if oxygen is available for all occupants, or make an emergency descent [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]
Engine fire
The airplane may be structurally damaged and may still be burning; it is expendable, and only the people aboard matter [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]

A high-speed descent could blow out the fire, but weakened structure is a major concern and a low-airspeed descent puts less stress on it [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. A single-engine airplane with the fuel off has to make a forced landing [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]
Other: electrical fire
Burning materials may continue to burn after the circuit is off [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]
The most prudent course is to land as soon as possible [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]

body.p: Engine fire has one more trap worth a separate sentence in your brief: fires that appear to be out have been known to rekindle with changes in airflow pattern and airspeed [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]. So the speed you pick is not only a structural choice.

Teaching tip (application): give the learner the situation, then ask two questions before anything moves. 'Where are we going: down to an altitude, or to the ground?' and 'What is our speed ceiling in this configuration?' A learner who can answer both has understood K2, not just memorized it.

callout.text: Pressure: mask, then down. Smoke: masks, down, and think before gear and flaps. Fire: down to land, and easy on a hurt airframe [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]] [[24:359|AFH 18-10]] [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

check.q: For each of the three ACS situations, what comes first, before or while the nose goes down?
check.a: Depressurization: oxygen [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]. Severe cabin smoke: oxygen masks if available and an immediate descent [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]. Engine fire: unless the POH says otherwise, mixture to idle cutoff and fuel selector off [[24:358|AFH 18-9]].

chunks.title: Immediate action items, checklists and ATC

body.p: The ACS expects checklist use, but it accepts that in some situations reading the checklist is impractical or unsafe. Then the evaluator assesses the published or recommended immediate action memory items, and the review of the checklist once conditions permit; in a single-pilot airplane the checklist is reviewed after the elements are done (CFI ACS Appendix 2). Teach that sequence on purpose: memory items, fly the descent, then the checklist.

bullets: Engine fire, unless the AFM/POH directs otherwise: mixture to idle cutoff and fuel selector off, ignition left on to burn the fuel left in the lines; if the flames go out, do not restart [[24:358|AFH 18-9]].

Master switch: some checklists call for it, but unless the fire is electrical or a crash landing is imminent, turning it off removes the panel radios for distress calls and ATC loses the transponder return [[24:358|AFH 18-9]].
Electrical fire: try to find and isolate the faulty circuit; if you cannot, and flight conditions permit, turn the battery master and alternator off [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].
Cabin fire: identify and shut down the faulty system; use the extinguisher first, then open the vents; close them at once if the smoke increases [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].
Your airplane's POH Section 3 is the real list. Have the learner write the memory items for your airplane and say them from memory before the flight (application).

body.p: ATC and the rules. In an emergency requiring immediate action, the pilot in command may deviate from any rule of part 91 to the extent required [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3]]. A pilot who deviates from an ATC clearance that way must notify ATC as soon as possible and obtain an amended clearance [[34:28|AIM 6-1-1]]. If unable to establish communications right away, squawk 7700 [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]]. Declaring an emergency gets additional assistance and priority handling [[30:47|RMH 6-4]].

But the RMH is honest about timing: ATC help is useful when lost, yet there may be no time to contact ATC in an emergency, and the pilot has to prioritize tasks and manage workload [[30:56|RMH 8-3]]. Teach the order: aviate (memory items and the descent), then talk.

callout.text: Application: in training, have the learner touch and name each memory item ("mixture, idle cutoff, simulated") rather than moving it. You get to see that the sequence is right without creating a real emergency.

check.q: The evaluator watches you roll into the descent and asks why you have not read the checklist yet. What does the ACS say about that?
check.a: When reading the checklist is impractical or unsafe, the evaluator assesses the immediate action memory items and the checklist review once conditions permit; single-pilot, the checklist is reviewed after the elements are done (CFI ACS Appendix 2).

chunks.title: The procedure, and how the scenario sets the configuration

body.p: The AFH procedure, except when the manufacturer prohibits it [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]:

bullets: Power to idle.
Propeller control, if equipped, to low pitch (high rpm), so the propeller acts as an aerodynamic brake against excessive airspeed buildup.
Landing gear and flaps extended as the manufacturer recommends, for maximum drag, so the descent is as rapid as possible without excessive airspeed.
Bank of about 30 to 45 degrees on entry, in a turn, at the maximum allowable airspeed for the procedure, which gives more drag and a high descent rate.

body.p: Chapter 3 of the AFH frames it the same way from another angle: some airplanes have a specific emergency descent procedure in the AFM/POH; in general these are high-drag, high-airspeed procedures with a specific configuration (for example power idle, propellers forward, gear extended and flaps retracted) and a specific emergency descent airspeed, and they often include turns [[24:82|AFH 3-21]].

Configuring the airplane (R3) is where the scenario matters. The ACS asks for the airspeed and configuration "appropriate to the scenario specified by the evaluator and as covered in" the POH/AFM (CFI ACS AI.XII.A.S2). So the same airplane can be configured differently on two descents:

head: Scenario
Configuration thinking
Source
rows: Depressurization, airframe sound
The POH emergency descent configuration for maximum drag, at its maximum allowable speed
Cabin smoke
Gear and/or flaps may aggravate cabin smoke on some airplanes; follow the POH smoke procedure
Engine fire or suspected structural damage
A low-airspeed descent puts less stress on a weakened structure; control could be lost at any moment
Turbulence
VA limits apply on top of the configuration limits

callout.text: Any extended surface brings its own ceiling: VLE with the gear down and VFE with flaps out [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. A learner who drops the flaps from habit has just lowered the top of their speed range to the white arc [[24:389|AFH G-17]].

check.q: Where does AFH chapter 3 say the emergency descent configuration and airspeed come from, and what does it say they usually look like?
check.a: The AFM/POH specifies the procedure; in general it is a high-drag, high-airspeed procedure with a specific configuration and a specific emergency descent airspeed, often with turns [[24:82|AFH 3-21]].

chunks.title: Airspeed limits as the AFH frames them

body.p: The AFH gives the rule in three parts: do not let the airspeed pass VNE, VLE or VFE, as applicable; in turbulent conditions also comply with the VA limitations; and descend at the maximum allowable airspeed consistent with the procedure used [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. Your learner's ceiling is the lowest limit that applies right now.

head: Limit
What it is
Where you find it
When it is the ceiling
rows: VNE
Never-exceed speed; operating above it may cause damage or structural failure [[24:389|AFH G-17]]
Red line [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]]
Always; clean, smooth air
VNO and the yellow arc
Top of the green arc; above it, smooth air only, with caution [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]]
Green and yellow arcs [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]]
Not a hard limit in smooth air, but a warning sign if the air is rough
VFE
Maximum speed with the flaps extended [[24:389|AFH G-17]]
Top of the white arc [[24:389|AFH G-17]]
Flaps out
VFO
Maximum speed to extend or retract the flaps [[24:389|AFH G-17]]
AFM/POH
While the flaps move
VLO
Maximum speed to operate the gear through its cycle [[24:247|AFH 12-16]]
AFM/POH and placards, maybe not on the dial [[24:247|AFH 12-16]]
While the gear moves
VLE
Maximum speed with the gear extended [[24:247|AFH 12-16]]
AFM/POH and placards [[24:247|AFH 12-16]]
Gear down
VA
The rough-air speed and maximum speed for abrupt maneuvers; it changes with weight [[24:389|AFH G-17]]
AFM/POH and placards [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]]
Turbulence

body.p: Read the placard with your learner. In the AFH example, the gear may go down at up to 129 KIAS and may stay extended up to 129 KIAS, but gear up is limited to 107 KIAS [[24:247|AFH 12-16]]. Gear operating limits are there because airstream loads at higher speeds can damage the gear components [[24:247|AFH 12-16]]. Application: the lower retraction number is the one that catches people during the cleanup after the level-off.

Turbulence: gust load factors increase with airspeed; in extremely rough air reduce to design maneuvering speed, and some gusts may exceed the load limits at any speed held [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]]. VA itself moves with weight: the PHAK example is 100 knots heavy but only 90 knots light [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]].

callout.text: +0/-10 knots (CFI ACS AI.XII.A.S5): the target is a ceiling, not a center. Pick the lowest limit that applies, then fly at or a little under it.

check.q: Your learner lowers the gear in a retractable single, then accelerates. Which two gear speeds apply, and in what order?
check.a: VLO first, because the gear may only be operated through its cycle below it; then, once extended, VLE becomes the ceiling. Both come from the AFM/POH and placards, not necessarily the dial [[24:247|AFH 12-16]].

chunks.title: Performance and limits: bank, load factor and structure

body.p: Why a turn with 30 to 45 degrees of bank, and not a push: the bank is there to keep the load factor positive [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. When the elevator is snapped forward, the load factor can drop toward zero and below, the 'floating free' feeling, with negative loads that lift the pilot from the seat [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]]. Rolling in and letting the nose fall in the turn gets the airplane pointing down without that push (application).

Why not steeper than 45 degrees: load factors become significant to both flight performance and the load on the wing structure as the bank increases beyond about 45 degrees [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]]. In a level turn, 45 degrees gives 1.41 G and 60 degrees gives 2.0, and stalling speed rises with the square root of the load factor [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

bullets: Limit loads: normal category +3.8 to -1.52, utility +4.4 to -1.76 [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]]. The negative limits are much smaller, which is one more reason not to push over.
Above the positive limit load, objectionable permanent deformation and a high rate of fatigue damage can occur [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]].
Abrupt pull-ups at high diving speeds may impose critical loads on the structure [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]], which is exactly where an emergency descent ends.

VA protects only one full control input, one time, in one axis, in smooth air; not several full inputs in one axis, or full inputs in more than one axis at once [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]]. Rapid, large alternating inputs may cause structural failure at any speed [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100f]].

Engine: high-speed descents can shock cool the engine with abrupt temperature changes [[1:177|PHAK 7-17]], and prolonged practice should be avoided to prevent excessive cooling of the cylinders [[24:358|AFH 18-9]].

body.p: For the full Vg diagram and the limit and ultimate load story, send the learner to the Commercial lesson (CA.IX.A). Your job here is to make the link: high speed plus an abrupt pull is the dangerous corner of this maneuver.

check.q: A learner asks why the bank range stops at 45 degrees. What do the PHAK and AFH give you to answer with?
check.a: Beyond about 45 degrees, load factors become significant to performance and wing loads [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]]. A level 60 degree bank already means 2.0 G, and the stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

chunks.title: The recovery: lead it, roll level, raise the nose gently

body.p: Start the recovery at a high enough altitude to ensure a safe recovery back to level flight or a precautionary landing [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. In training, once the descent is established and stabilized, terminate it [[24:358|AFH 18-9]]. On the checkride the evaluator specifies the level-off altitude, and the tolerance is ±100 feet (CFI ACS AI.XII.A.S5).

Lead the level-off. The IFH rule is to lead by an altitude equal to 10 percent of the rate of descent, so at 1,000 fpm start 100 feet above the target [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]. A late pitch change tends to overshoot the altitude unless it is made with a rapid movement, and rapid changes can lead to control issues or spatial disorientation [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]. Emergency descent rates are high, so the 10 percent lead is large; work it out on the ground for your airplane (application).

The pull-out is where airframes get hurt. A startled pilot who pulls back rapidly while rolling to wings level can create loads that damage or fail the airframe; the design limit is exceeded more easily in a rolling pullout [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]. Near VNE, control inputs are made slowly and gently [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]. The spiral dive template is written for an upset, but its order is the model for this recovery.

bullets: Roll wings level with coordinated aileron and rudder, then gently raise the nose to level flight [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].

Power: on an ordinary descent level-off to cruise, the IFH adds power before raising the nose [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]. From an emergency descent you are already faster than cruise, so add power as the speed comes back (application).
Clean up only below the limits: gear below VLO [[24:247|AFH 12-16]], flaps below VFO [[24:389|AFH G-17]].
Hold the specified altitude ±100 feet (CFI ACS AI.XII.A.S5).

callout.text: From the right seat, keep your hand near the yoke during the level-off. If the learner starts a hard rolling pull, you have a second or two to stop it [[24:131|AFH 5-26]] [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

check.q: Your learner levels off 180 ft below the specified altitude after a late, hard pull. Which IFH points explain both the miss and the danger?
check.a: A late pitch change tends to overshoot the altitude unless made with a rapid movement, and rapid changes can lead to control issues or spatial disorientation; lead by about 10 percent of the descent rate [[23:211|IFH 7-50]].

chunks.title: Where it ends: altitude, wind, terrain and the landing spot

body.p: Every emergency descent ends at a lower altitude or on the ground [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. Teach the learner to name the end before the nose goes down. R1 lists the things that decide it (CFI ACS AI.XII.A.R1):

bullets: Altitude: start the recovery high enough for a safe recovery to level flight or a precautionary landing [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. The sources give no minimum practice altitude for this maneuver (see gaps).

Wind: when there is time to maneuver, wind direction and velocity govern the approach plan [[24:353|AFH 18-4]]. Groundspeed matters most in a crash: doubling it quadruples the destructive energy [[24:352|AFH 18-3]].

Terrain: the choice of site depends on the route, the height above the ground when the emergency happens, and excess airspeed, which can be converted into distance and/or altitude [[24:353|AFH 18-4]]. An emergency descent ends with plenty of excess airspeed.
Obstructions: obstacles in the final approach path govern the plan; it is sometimes better to approach over an unobstructed area regardless of wind [[24:353|AFH 18-4]] [[24:354|AFH 18-5]].

Gliding distance: glide ratio is the distance traveled for the altitude lost, for example 10 to 1 [[24:82|AFH 3-21]]. With an engine fire and the fuel off, a single-engine airplane is gliding to a forced landing [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

Available landing distance: dimensions and slope of the field are part of the plan [[24:353|AFH 18-4]]. If smoke keeps the flaps up, remember a no-flap landing needs substantially more runway, as much as 50 percent more [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

body.p: A precautionary landing is generally less hazardous than a forced landing: more time to choose terrain and plan, and power to correct errors. Too many precautionary situations become forced landings through wishful thinking [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].

callout.text: Teaching move from the AIH: prompt the learner to identify hazards and a safe place for an emergency landing, and to say their thinking out loud [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]. In this maneuver, ask for the field during the first 90 degrees of turn.

check.q: Your learner has smoke in the cabin and leaves the flaps up per the POH. What does that change about the landing they are descending toward?
check.a: It becomes a no-flap landing, which needs substantially more runway, as much as 50 percent more [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]; the field dimensions are part of the approach plan [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

chunks.title: Collision hazards: clearing above, around and below

body.p: This maneuver drops the airplane through thousands of feet of other people's airspace in a minute or two. The defense starts before it does.

bullets: Clearing turns make sure the next maneuver does not go into another aircraft's flightpath; with good visual scanning they are the most effective strategy for collision avoidance. The instructor should teach an effective clearing procedure and insist on its use [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].
Flying the simulated descent in a turn lets the pilot check for traffic below and look for a landing area; a radio call announcing the descent may be appropriate [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].
Training airspace may be crowded, often with haze, which adds to the collision hazard. The instructor and learner are both responsible for the lookout [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

Some airplanes have an Emergency Autoland system; it takes no evasive action, so avoid the path of any aircraft under its control or suspected to be [[24:33|AFH 1-12]]. An automated emergency descent mode may turn its aircraft up to 90 degrees and descend [[34:340|AIM PCG E-1]].

Transponder: in a real emergency, 7700 normally triggers an alarm or special indicator at all control positions [[34:29|AIM 6-2-2]]. In practice, do not dial it in; even passing through 7700 by mistake causes false alarms [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20]].

body.p: Teaching it (application): the descent goes down and turns, so clear the turn direction and below. In a high-wing airplane, raise the wing before you roll in. In a low-wing, the area below the nose and wing is hidden; clearing turns in both directions show it.

callout.text: Say it, then do it: "Clear left, clear right, clear below, landing area at our ten o'clock." Make the learner say the same words every time [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].

check.q: During practice, your learner reaches for the transponder to set 7700 'to make it realistic.' What do you tell them?
check.a: No. Code 7700 normally triggers an alarm or special indicator at all ATC control positions [[34:29|AIM 6-2-2]], and even inadvertent selection causes false alarms [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20]]. Say it, do not set it.

body.p: R4 names four things: distractions, task prioritization, loss of situational awareness, and disorientation (CFI ACS AI.XII.A.R4). An emergency descent piles all four on at once.

bullets: Distractions: the evaluator should add realistic distractions to see how you divide attention inside and outside the flight deck (CFI ACS Appendix 2). Expect a smoke or fire scenario plus a question in the middle of the turn.

Task prioritization: in an emergency, a pilot needs to prioritize tasks and manage workload; there may be no time for ATC [[30:56|RMH 8-3]]. Airborne, budgeting time and prioritizing tasks give time to finish tasks without error [[30:47|RMH 6-4]].

Loss of situational awareness: the RMH list is aircraft position, flight path, other aircraft, the environment and the human factors in play [[30:47|RMH 6-4]]. A learner deep in the checklist loses all five.

Disorientation: after a long turn, a head movement in another plane (looking for a checklist, an extinguisher, a dropped item) can cause the Coriolis illusion. Keep head movement minimal [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].

body.p: The graveyard spiral is the illusion trap of a long descending turn: in a prolonged coordinated turn the pilot feels no turn, and on rolling out feels a turn the other way and may roll back into it; pulling back to stop the descent then tightens the spiral [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]. Smoke or haze that hides the horizon makes this real. A rapid throttle reduction can also give a disoriented pilot the urge to pull the nose up (somatogravic illusion) [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].

The mind is a hazard too. Reluctance to accept the emergency leads to delay and indecision, and desperate attempts to correct what went wrong at the expense of airplane control fall in the same category [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].

callout.text: To spot fixation, try to follow the learner's eyes: a gaze stuck on one instrument suggests fixation, and a gaze that never reaches the engine gauges suggests inattention [[25:82|AIH 3-31]].

check.q: During a long descending turn in haze, your learner bends down to find the checklist and suddenly feels the airplane tumbling. What happened, and what do you teach?
check.a: The Coriolis illusion: after a long turn, a head movement in a different plane can create the illusion of turning on another axis. Teach minimal head movement and a cross-check that keeps the head still [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].

chunks.title: Simulated or real: briefing and flying the practice safely

body.p: The ACS sets the principle: safety of flight comes first, and if performing aspects of a maneuver such as emergency procedures would jeopardize safety, the evaluator will ask for that portion to be simulated (CFI ACS Appendix 2). Your brief should say, item by item, what is real and what is only touched and named.

head: Item
In practice
Why
rows: Power idle, propeller high rpm, bank 30 to 45 degrees
Real
This is the maneuver [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]
Gear and flaps
Real, per the POH, within VLO, VLE, VFE
The configuration is part of the Task [[24:357|AFH 18-8]] (CFI ACS AI.XII.A.S2)
Mixture idle cutoff, fuel selector off
Simulated
After an engine fire, the AFH says no restart should be attempted [[24:358|AFH 18-9]]; in practice the engine must keep running (application)
Master switch off
Simulated
It removes the radios and ATC's transponder return [[24:358|AFH 18-9]]
MAYDAY and 7700
Simulated (said, not sent)
7700 triggers alarms at all control positions [[34:29|AIM 6-2-2]]
Advisory radio call
Real, if appropriate
It alerts other aircraft [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]

bullets: Throttle control: for simulated emergency landings the AFH says either the instructor or the pilot has complete control of the throttle, with no doubt, because many near accidents have come from such misunderstandings. It also says to keep the engine warm and cleared [[24:200|AFH 9-29]]. Brief the same for this maneuver (application).
Controls: brief the positive exchange of flight controls before flight [[25:178|AIH 9-8]] (CFI ACS Appendix 2).
Engine: terminate once the descent is stabilized; prolonged practice can cool the cylinders too much [[24:358|AFH 18-9]].

Altitude and weather: do not teach a maneuver at an inappropriate altitude, such as stalls below a cloud layer without room to recover [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]. The descent needs room above the level-off for the lead and the recovery.
People on the ground: a simulated emergency landing approach is terminated before it creates an undue hazard or annoyance to persons or property on the ground [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].

callout.text: Simulated engine failures done incorrectly have created real emergencies and caused accidents [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]. The same goes for any 'simulated' fire item that someone actually moves. Say "simulated" every time.

check.q: Why does the instructor brief the fuel selector and mixture as 'touch and name' items in this maneuver?
check.a: Because the real engine fire action cuts the fuel, and the AFH says no restart should be attempted once the flames are out [[24:358|AFH 18-9]]; when performing an emergency procedure would jeopardize safety, it is simulated (CFI ACS Appendix 2).

body.p: Ground first, then the airplane. The AIH's low-fuel example starts the scenario in the classroom until the learner's answers are consistent, then flies it [[25:82|AIH 3-31]]. Do the same here: give each K2 situation in the classroom and have the learner say the memory items, the configuration and the speed ceiling.

head: Building block
Where it comes from
rows: Steep turns: bank control, load factor, overbanking
Lesson AI.IX.A; [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]
Descents and level-offs with a lead
Lesson AI.XI.C; [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]
Airspeed limits for this airplane at today's weight
Fire, smoke and decompression knowledge
Lessons PA.IX.A and CA.IX.A; [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]
The emergency descent itself, then inside a scenario

body.p: Demonstrate it the way you want it flown. Explain the power settings and attitudes as you fly, in the same order you briefed them, and include every safety procedure, because learners imitate the instructor [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. A sample narration (application): 'Clear left, right and below. Field at our ten o'clock. Simulated smoke: masks on, simulated. Power idle, prop forward. Rolling into 40 degrees, nose comes down in the turn. Gear down below VLO. Ceiling is VLE because the flaps stay up for smoke. Target 125, I'm at 123. Level-off at 4,500: I start at 4,700.'

Then let the learner talk you through it while you fly; it frees them from flying and shows you whether they understand, so a misconception can be fixed before they are busy controlling the airplane [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. When they fly it, be ready to take control, especially on the first attempt [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

Make it a scenario. Scenario-based training integrates maneuvers into realistic flight situations once they are learned [[25:143|AIH 6-12]]. Simulated emergencies and heavy workload are valuable for assessing a learner's judgment, and SRM is graded as explain, practice, or manage/decide [[25:32|AIH 1-28]]. A good final goal (application): smoke on a cross-country, where the learner chooses the configuration, the field and the call without prompting.

callout.text: Application: never introduce the emergency descent and a real emergency landing in the same first lesson. Let the descent and level-off be clean at altitude before any scenario ends near the ground.

check.q: Why put the classroom version of the smoke scenario before the first flight demonstration?
check.a: The AIH low-fuel example uses the classroom first, until the learner's answers are consistent and insightful, and only then flies the scenario [[25:82|AIH 3-31]]. Here that means the memory items, configuration and speed ceiling are settled before the airplane is involved.

body.p: The AFH has no error list for the emergency descent itself. This table uses its lists for descents and descending turns [[24:85|AFH 3-24]] and steep spirals [[24:213|AFH 10-4]], plus the emergency descent text. On the checkride the evaluator may fly as your learner and make these errors for you to analyze and correct (CFI ACS AI.XII.A.S7).

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Failure to adequately clear for traffic in the turn direction or descent [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]
Rolls in without looking below or toward the turn
Clearing turns and a look below before rolling in [[24:33|AFH 1-12]] [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]
Pushing over instead of rolling into the bank
Items float, learner rises off the seat
Roll to 30 to 45 degrees and let the nose fall in the turn; keep the G positive [[24:357|AFH 18-8]] [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]]
Failure to maintain constant bank angle [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]
Bank creeping past 45 degrees, nose dropping, speed jumping
Fix the bank first; the speed follows (CFI ACS AI.XII.A.S4)
Inability to stabilize the glide, chasing the airspeed indicator [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]
Pitch pumping, speed swinging over the ceiling
Hold an attitude, small corrections, aim at or just under the ceiling (CFI ACS AI.XII.A.S5)
Inadequate airspeed control [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]: passing VFE, VLE or VNE
Flaps out above the white arc; gear lowered above VLO
Brief the lowest applicable limit before flight [[24:357|AFH 18-8]] [[24:247|AFH 12-16]]
Keeping a high speed in turbulence
Bumps grow, speed near the yellow arc
Slow to VA or the POH figure in rough air [[24:357|AFH 18-8]] [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]]
Skidding or slipping in the turn [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]
Ball out, especially at idle
Rudder to center the ball; feel the different rudder force without power
Becoming disoriented [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]
Loses track of heading and the field, head down
Outside references, minimal head movement, name the field again [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]
Late level-off and a hard rolling pull
Altitude missed, heavy G while rolling
Lead by 10 percent of the descent rate; roll level, then raise the nose gently [[23:211|IFH 7-50]] [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]
Head-down checklist during the turn
Bank and speed wander while reading
Memory items, fly the descent, checklist once conditions permit (CFI ACS Appendix 2)
Holding the practice descent too long
Long idle descent, cooling engine
Terminate once established and stable [[24:358|AFH 18-9]]
Slow to commit
Discusses the problem while still level
Reluctance to accept the emergency leads to delay and indecision; act [[24:350|AFH 18-1]]

body.p: Find the cause, not just the symptom. When the learner thinks out loud, you can tell an error that comes from a misconception ("flaps help it go down faster, so they always go out") from one that is a simple lack of motor skill [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

callout.text: Application: in the debrief, ask the learner which limit was their ceiling on that descent and why. If they cannot say, the speed error was a knowledge error, and more flying will not fix it.

check.q: Your learner's bank creeps from 40 to 55 degrees during the descent and the airspeed runs over the target. What is the AFH name for the error, and what do you fix first?
check.a: Failure to maintain constant bank angle [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]. Fix the bank back inside 30 to 45 degrees first (CFI ACS AI.XII.A.S4); the steeper bank drops the nose and the speed follows it.

f1.caption: Figure 18-6. Emergency descent. (AFH 18-9)
f1.alt: A high-wing airplane in a steep left bank begins a curving descent, shown by an orange path sweeping down and away over green farm fields, a road with utility poles, a farmhouse and distant brown hills.

f2.caption: Figure 8-8. Single engine airspeed indicator (ASI). (PHAK 8-9)
f2.alt: An airspeed indicator in knots with orange labels pointing to its markings: the white arc from VS0 to VFE, the green arc from VS1 to VNO, the yellow arc above it, and the red VNE line at the top of the yellow arc.

f3.caption: Figure 12-15. Placarded gear speeds in the flight deck. (AFH 12-16)
f3.alt: A dark placard reading GEAR DOWN 129 KIAS (MAX), GEAR UP 107 KIAS (MAX), EXTENDED 129 KIAS (MAX).

f4.caption: Figure 5-18. Spiral dive recovery template. (AFH 5-27)
f4.alt: A five-step table: 1, reduce power to idle; 2, apply some forward elevator; 3, roll wings level; 4, gently raise the nose to level flight; 5, increase power to climb power.

f5.alt: Drawing of a high-wing airplane's paths. A dashed blue oval is labeled Correct path. A wide red descending curve labeled Graveyard spiral ends at a crash burst, and a blue corkscrew labeled Graveyard spin also ends there. A second airplane flies off to the lower left.

f6.alt: A graph of load factor in G units from 0 to 7 against bank angle from 0 to 90 degrees. The red curve starts at 1 G, rises slowly to about 1.4 G at 45 degrees and 2 G at 60 degrees, then shoots up steeply past 4 G near 75 degrees and off the top of the chart past 80 degrees.

scenario.title: Smoke over the ridge, and the lesson after
scenario.setup: You are a CFI. Today your private pilot learner meets the emergency descent in an unpressurized, retractable-gear single with a constant-speed propeller. Placards: gear operating 140 KIAS, gear extended 160 KIAS, flaps extended 110 KIAS; VA 120 KIAS at maximum weight; red line 200 KIAS. The POH emergency descent is power idle, propeller full forward, gear down, flaps up, 155 KIAS. You are two aboard with half fuel. The practice area's highest terrain is 1,800 ft MSL, there is light to moderate chop below 5,000 ft, and a small airport lies 8 NM east. You start at 7,500 ft MSL.

questions.q: On the ground the learner says, 'The ceiling is 155, the POH says so.' What do you add about the forecast chop?
questions.a: In turbulent conditions the pilot also has to comply with the VA limitations [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. VA changes with weight, and two aboard with half fuel is lighter than the 120 KIAS placard weight [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]], so in the chop the speed has to come down below 155, using the POH turbulent air information if it has it [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]].

questions.q: You call 'Simulated: severe smoke in the cabin.' What should the learner do first, and does the POH descent configuration still fit?
questions.a: Oxygen masks if available and an immediate descent [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]. On some airplanes lowering the gear and/or flaps can aggravate cabin smoke [[24:359|AFH 18-10]], so the learner should check the POH smoke procedure against the gear-down descent; the configuration must fit the scenario and the POH (CFI ACS AI.XII.A.S2).

questions.q: Rolling in, the learner reaches for the master switch 'because it is on the smoke checklist.' What do you say, and why?
questions.a: Touch it and say it; do not switch it off. Turning the master off removes the panel radios and ATC loses the transponder return [[24:358|AFH 18-9]], and when an emergency procedure would jeopardize safety it is simulated (CFI ACS Appendix 2).

questions.q: In the descent the bank creeps to 50 degrees and the airspeed reads 166 KIAS with the gear down. Analyze and correct it.
questions.a: Two errors: failure to maintain constant bank angle [[24:85|AFH 3-24]] and passing VLE, which the AFH says not to do [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. Shallow the bank to 30 to 45 degrees (CFI ACS AI.XII.A.S4) and gently raise the nose to get under 160; the +0 tolerance means any overshoot is out (CFI ACS AI.XII.A.S5). If it keeps building, take the controls [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

questions.q: You specify a level-off at 4,500 ft MSL. The VSI shows 2,400 fpm. Where should the learner start, and how?
questions.a: 10 percent of 2,400 fpm is 240 ft, so start about 4,740 ft MSL [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]. Roll wings level first, then raise the nose gently, because a rolling pullout exceeds the design limit more easily [[24:131|AFH 5-26]], and finish within ±100 feet (CFI ACS AI.XII.A.S5).

questions.q: In the debrief you ask: 'If that smoke had been real, where were we going?' What should a good answer include?
questions.a: The airport 8 NM east as a precautionary landing, generally less hazardous than a forced landing because of time and power [[24:350|AFH 18-1]]; the excess airspeed at the bottom converted into distance [[24:353|AFH 18-4]]; wind, field dimensions and obstacles [[24:353|AFH 18-4]]; and if the flaps stay up for smoke, a no-flap landing needing as much as 50 percent more runway [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

skills.do: "Clear the area." Clearing turns and a spoken look at and below your altitude and toward the turn, while you explain why this maneuver needs a look below.
skills.practice: Use the same clearing words before every descent with another instructor, and add the landing field to them [[24:33|AFH 1-12]] [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

skills.do: "Establish and maintain the appropriate airspeed and configuration appropriate to the scenario specified by the evaluator and as covered in Pilot's Operating Handbook (POH)/Airplane Flight Manual (AFM) for the emergency descent." Say the configuration and the speed ceiling for the scenario before you roll in.
skills.practice: Write each K2 scenario on a card with your airplane's configuration and ceiling, and drill them on the ground [[24:357|AFH 18-8]] [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

skills.do: "Maintain orientation, divide attention appropriately, and plan and execute a smooth recovery." Keep the field and the heading in your narration, and recover with wings level before the nose comes up.
skills.practice: Fly descents with a planned level-off and a field to point at, roll level then pull gently, and keep head movement small [[24:131|AFH 5-26]] [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].

skills.do: "Use bank angle between 30° and 45° to maintain positive load factors during the descent." Hold it steady while you talk.
skills.practice: Practice the roll-in at 30, 40 and 45 degrees and call the bank aloud while speaking about something else [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

skills.do: "Maintain appropriate airspeed +0/-10 knots, and level off at a specified altitude ±100 feet." Fly at or just under the lowest applicable limit and lead the level-off.
skills.practice: Before each practice, write the target, the lowest limit that applies and the lead altitude for your expected descent rate [[24:357|AFH 18-8]] [[23:211|IFH 7-50]].

skills.do: "Complete the appropriate checklist(s)." Memory items first, the descent, then the checklist review once conditions permit (CFI ACS Appendix 2).
skills.practice: Say your airplane's fire, smoke and descent memory items from memory, then run the printed checklist at level flight [[24:358|AFH 18-9]].

skills.do: "Analyze and correct common errors related to this Task." When the evaluator, as your learner, pushes over, overbanks or overspeeds, name the error, say why it matters and give the fix, taking the controls if needed.
skills.practice: Have another instructor fly the errors from the table in this lesson while you call and correct them from the right seat [[24:85|AFH 3-24]] [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

quiz.q: Which elements does the CFI emergency descent Task add that the commercial Task does not have?
options: A tighter airspeed tolerance of +0/-5 knots and a narrower bank range of 30° to 40°
K1 purpose and procedures, K6 common errors, and S7 analyze and correct errors
A required simulated MAYDAY call and a level-off within ±50 feet of the specified altitude
A demonstration entered from at least 5,000 ft AGL and an oral check of every POH speed
quiz.why: The bank, airspeed and level-off lines are word for word the same; the CFI Task adds K1, K6 and S7 (CFI ACS AI.XII.A; Commercial ACS CA.IX.A).

quiz.q: In AFH chapter 3's example of a typical emergency descent configuration, where are the flaps?
options: Extended to the first notch, for a little extra drag without a low VFE
Fully extended, for the maximum drag the airplane can make at that speed
Retracted, with the gear extended and power at idle
Extended only after the airspeed is below VA, then left down to landing
quiz.why: The example is power idle, propellers forward, gear extended and flaps retracted, at a specific emergency descent airspeed [[24:82|AFH 3-21]].

quiz.q: A pressurized single has intense smoke that the pressurization air is not clearing. What two options does the AFH give?
options: Open the foul weather window, or climb to clear the smoke
Shut off the pressurization, then hold altitude until it clears
Turn the battery master off, or descend at best glide speed
Depressurize at altitude if everyone has oxygen, or make an emergency descent
quiz.why: If smoke is intense it may be necessary to depressurize at altitude, if oxygen is available for all occupants, or to execute an emergency descent [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

quiz.q: How does the AFH define VLO?
options: The maximum speed for operating the landing gear through its cycle
The maximum speed at which the airplane may be flown with the gear extended
The minimum speed at which the gear warning horn will sound at idle power
The lowest speed at which the emergency system can extend the gear fully
quiz.why: VLO is the maximum landing gear operating speed, for operating the gear through its cycle; VLE is for flight with the gear extended [[24:247|AFH 12-16]].

quiz.q: What does the AFH glossary call VFO?
options: The maximum speed with the flaps fully extended and locked
The maximum speed at which the flaps can be extended or retracted
The lowest speed at which full flaps may be selected in turbulence
The flap speed marked at the bottom of the white arc
quiz.why: VFO is the maximum speed that the flaps can be extended or retracted; VFE is the maximum speed with flaps extended, the top of the white arc [[24:389|AFH G-17]].

quiz.q: Your learner snaps the throttle to idle in haze to start the descent. Which illusion does the IFH tie to a rapid throttle reduction?
options: Coriolis illusion, felt as turning on a different axis after a head movement in the turn
Elevator illusion, felt as a climb after an updraft lifts the airplane suddenly
Somatogravic illusion, which can lead a disoriented pilot to pull the nose up
Inversion illusion, felt as tumbling backward after an abrupt change from a climb
quiz.why: A rapid deceleration by quick reduction of the throttle can make a disoriented pilot pull the aircraft into a nose-up or stall attitude [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].

quiz.q: During the descent your learner's eyes never leave the airspeed indicator, and they never glance at the engine gauges. What does the AIH say each pattern can point to?
options: One instrument stared at suggests fixation; engine gauges never checked suggest inattention
Both patterns are a normal scan for a high-speed descent, since airspeed is the primary instrument
One instrument stared at shows good attention; engine gauges skipped show the learner trusts them
Both patterns suggest the learner is ready for a scenario with distractions added in the turn
quiz.why: Learners who look at one instrument for an extended time might have a fixation problem, and those whose gaze never reaches the engine instruments might have an inattention problem [[25:82|AIH 3-31]].

quiz.q: According to the AIM, what normally happens at a radar facility when a transponder shows code 7700?
options: Nothing happens until the pilot also transmits a call on 121.5 MHz
Only the supervisor's position is alerted, and only after a few minutes
The code is ignored unless the aircraft is inside Class B or C airspace
An alarm or special indicator appears at all control positions
quiz.why: Radar facilities are equipped so that code 7700 normally triggers an alarm or special indicator at all control positions [[34:29|AIM 6-2-2]].

quiz.q: Smoke forces you to leave your IFR altitude without a clearance. What does the AIM say you must do about the clearance?
options: Nothing; an emergency cancels the clearance automatically
Notify ATC as soon as possible and obtain an amended clearance
File a written report within 24 hours before any further flight
Return to the assigned altitude as soon as the smoke clears
quiz.why: If the emergency authority of 14 CFR 91.3(b) is used to deviate from a clearance, the pilot in command must notify ATC as soon as possible and obtain an amended clearance [[34:28|AIM 6-1-1]].

quiz.q: Why do airplanes with retractable gear have limiting speeds for gear operation?
options: Airstream loads at higher speeds may damage the gear components
The gear doors create too much drag for the engine above the white arc
The gear motor cannot draw enough current at high airspeeds to finish
The gear warning horn becomes unreliable above the top of the green arc
quiz.why: The operating loads on the gear at higher airspeeds may cause structural damage from the forces of the airstream, so limiting speeds protect the gear [[24:247|AFH 12-16]].

final_quiz.q: The evaluator, as your learner, gets 'simulated cabin smoke' and lowers full flaps out of habit before rolling in. Which response best covers the sources?
options: Fine: full flaps give the most drag, and drag is the goal of the maneuver
Fine, as long as the speed stays below VNE in smooth air
Raise them only if the evaluator says the smoke is from the engine
Flaps can aggravate cabin smoke on some airplanes, and they lower the ceiling to VFE; follow the POH
final_quiz.why: On some airplanes lowering gear and/or flaps can aggravate a cabin smoke problem [[24:359|AFH 18-10]], and with flaps out VFE is a limit not to pass [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner levels off at 125 KIAS with the gear down in an airplane placarded like AFH Figure 12-15 and moves the gear handle up right away. What is the problem?
options: None, because 125 KIAS is already below the 129 KIAS gear down limit on it
The gear up limit on that placard is 107 KIAS, so they should slow first
None, because the 129 KIAS extended limit on that placard also covers retraction
The gear should stay down until landing whenever the descent was for smoke
final_quiz.why: The placard shows gear down 129, gear up 107 and extended 129 KIAS [[24:247|AFH 12-16]]; VLO limits operating the gear through its cycle, so retraction waits until below 107 KIAS.

final_quiz.q: Below VA in the level-off, the evaluator-as-learner rocks the yoke fore and aft and rolls hard at the same time, saying 'below VA nothing can break.' What is the best correction?
options: Agree: any control input is safe below VA, which is exactly why VA is placarded in the cockpit
Agree, as long as the air is smooth and the airspeed is also below VNO, the top of the green arc
Disagree: VA covers one full input, one axis, once; large alternating or combined inputs can fail it
Disagree: control inputs are only limited above VNE, so the fix is simply to slow down further still
final_quiz.why: VA does not protect against multiple full inputs in one axis or full inputs in more than one axis at once [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]], and rapid, large alternating inputs may cause structural failure at any speed, even below VA [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100f]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner starts the descent wings level with a firm push on the yoke, and your headsets float. What do you tell them?
options: Good: a push gives the fastest start, and the ACS sets no bank requirement until the descent is stable
The push can make the load factor zero or negative; roll into 30 to 45 degrees of bank instead
Good, but only in an airplane that carries a utility category placard and is below its maximum weight
The push is fine if it is held for less than a second, so the engine is not shock cooled
final_quiz.why: Snapping the elevator forward can produce zero or negative load factors [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]]; the AFH bank of about 30 to 45 degrees keeps the load factor positive [[24:357|AFH 18-8]] (CFI ACS AI.XII.A.S4).

final_quiz.q: The VSI shows 2,500 fpm down and the specified level-off is 5,500 ft. Using the IFH lead, where do you start the level-off?
final_quiz.why: Lead by 10 percent of the rate of descent [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]: 0.10 x 2,500 = 250 ft; 5,500 + 250 = 5,750 ft.

final_quiz.q: An engine fire is out after you shut off the fuel. Which set of points does the AFH tell the pilot to keep in mind during the emergency descent?
options: It may be badly damaged and lose control at any moment, may still be burning, and is expendable
The engine may be restarted after two minutes, and the firewall protects the structure from damage
The descent must be flown at VNE to keep the fire out, and the airplane itself must be saved
Once the flames are out the fire cannot return, so normal descent speeds and maneuvering apply
final_quiz.why: The AFH lists that the airplane may be severely structurally damaged so control could be lost at any moment, may still be on fire, and is expendable [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

final_quiz.q: After two full turns of descent in haze, your learner rolls out, says the airplane feels banked the other way, rolls back into the old turn and pulls to stop the sink. What is happening?
options: The leans in reverse, which is harmless once the wings are level and the ball is centered
An elevator illusion caused by the rapid throttle reduction at the entry to the descent
A graveyard spiral: the pull tightens the spiral and adds to the altitude loss
Normal orientation: the airplane really is banked, and the learner's correction is right
final_quiz.why: In a prolonged coordinated turn the pilot feels no turn, feels a turn the other way on recovery, may return to the original turn, and pulling back tightens the spiral: the graveyard spiral [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].

final_quiz.q: There is a smell of burning insulation, and you cannot find the bad circuit. Conditions permit. What does the AFH say to do, and what should you still expect?
options: Leave everything on so ATC keeps the transponder return, and continue to the destination
Battery master and alternator off; what is already burning may keep burning, so land soon
Turn each switch back on in turn until the smell returns, then continue to the destination
Open every vent first to clear the smoke, and only then start looking for the faulty circuit
final_quiz.why: If the faulty circuit cannot be isolated and conditions permit, turn the battery master and alternator off; ignited materials may continue to burn, and the most prudent course is to land as soon as possible [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

final_quiz.q: With the master off, the smoke has stopped and the engine runs normally. Your learner wants to press on to the destination 60 NM away. Why does the AFH favor a precautionary landing now?
options: A forced landing is the less hazardous choice, so the AFH wants the pilot to land at once anywhere
The AFH forbids any further flight after an electrical failure, even when the engine is running
The engine will shock cool after the long idle descent, so it must be shut down on the ground soon
Time to choose and plan, and power to correct errors, before it becomes a forced landing
final_quiz.why: A precautionary landing is generally less hazardous than a forced landing: more time for terrain selection and planning, and power to compensate for errors; too many become forced landings through wishful thinking [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].

final_quiz.q: During your learner's first practice descent, both of you rest a hand near the throttle. What does the AFH guidance for simulated emergencies say about that?
options: Both pilots should hold the throttle so either can add power quickly
The instructor holds it only below 1,000 ft AGL
Either the instructor or the pilot has complete control of the throttle, with no doubt about who
The learner must never touch the throttle during simulated emergencies
final_quiz.why: During a simulated emergency landing, either the instructor or the pilot should have complete control of the throttle; many near accidents came from misunderstandings [[24:200|AFH 9-29]]. Application: brief the same here.

final_quiz.q: Before rolling in, which prompt does the AIH suggest that fits the start of an emergency descent?
options: Ask them to identify collision hazards and a safe place for an emergency landing
Ask them to recite the steps of the demonstration-performance method aloud first
Ask them to compute the true airspeed and descent rate they expect in the turn
Ask them to rate their readiness for the maneuver on a scale of one to five
final_quiz.why: The AIH suggests prompting learners to identify hazards and verbalize their thinking, for example to identify potential collision hazards and a safe place to make an emergency landing [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

final_quiz.q: The evaluator, as your learner, flies the descent with a 40 degree bank but the airspeed swings 8 knots over and under the target as they keep moving the nose. Name the error and the fix.
options: Failure to clear the area; add a second clearing turn before the next descent is started
Excessive rudder in the recovery from the turn; neutralize the pedals and use aileron only
Overbanking past the ACS range; roll out to about 20 degrees of bank and hold that until the level-off
Chasing the airspeed indicator; hold an attitude and make small corrections at or under target
final_quiz.why: Inability to stabilize the glide (chasing the airspeed indicator) is a listed descent error [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]; with a +0/-10 knot tolerance, any swing above the target is out (CFI ACS AI.XII.A.S5).

final_quiz.q: Severe smoke fills the cabin. Your learner says, 'First I'll call Center and ask for a lower altitude.' Which response fits the sources best?
options: Masks if available and start down now; there may be no time for ATC, so prioritize and call on the way
Call first: declaring an emergency gets priority, so the descent can wait
Climb first for better radio and radar coverage, then descend
Hold altitude and open the vents until Center answers
final_quiz.why: With severe smoke the pilot should start an immediate descent, using oxygen masks if available [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]; in an emergency there may be no time to contact ATC, so prioritize tasks [[30:56|RMH 8-3]].

takeaways: Purpose: down as soon and as fast as possible, without exceeding any structural limit.
Name the situation (depressurization, smoke, engine fire) and the end point before the nose goes down.
Power idle, propeller high rpm, gear and flaps per the POH and the scenario, 30 to 45 degrees of bank.
The ceiling is the lowest limit that applies: VNE, VLE, VFE, VLO and VFO while moving things, VA in turbulence.
+0/-10 knots and ±100 feet: aim at or under the ceiling, lead the level-off, roll level then pull gently.
Brief what is real and what is simulated; never move fuel, mixture, master or transponder for a 'simulated' fire.
Clear below, keep heads still in long turns, and terminate practice once the descent is stable.
cfi_notes: The AFH emergency descent text names VNE, VLE, VFE and, in turbulence, VA [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. It does not name VLO or VFO; those come from AFH 12-16 [[24:247|AFH 12-16]] and the glossary [[24:389|AFH G-17]]. Teach all of them, because the learner moves the gear and flaps during this maneuver.

AFH chapter 18 says to extend gear and flaps as the manufacturer recommends [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]; AFH chapter 3's example has the flaps retracted [[24:82|AFH 3-21]]. Not a conflict: both defer to the POH. Use the difference to ask the learner why a manufacturer might leave the flaps up.

PHAK 5-37 says no combination of maneuver and gust can create damage below maneuvering speed [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]], but PHAK 5-35 limits VA protection to one full input in one axis in smooth air [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]] and AC 61-67C warns of failures below VA from large alternating inputs [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100f]]. Teach the narrower statements.
The AFH sets the 30 to 45 degree bank 'when initiating the descent' [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]; the ACS asks for it during the descent (CFI ACS AI.XII.A.S4). Hold it all the way down on the checkride.
The AFH gives no level-off lead for this maneuver. Use the IFH 10 percent rule [[23:211|IFH 7-50]], which matches the AFH 10 percent example for a 1,000 fpm descent [[24:82|AFH 3-21]].

The AIM's emergency assistance list starts with 'climb, if possible' for communications and radar [[34:45|AIM 6-3-2]]. With fire, smoke or a decompression, the AFH and PHAK point down [[24:359|AFH 18-10]] [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]. Expect a sharp learner to ask about it.
The throttle control and terminate-before-hazard guidance comes from simulated emergency landings [[24:200|AFH 9-29]]; applying it here is your judgment, and a good one.

Learners mix this up with the steep spiral. The AFH notes similarities but says the reasons usually differ and the airspeed and configuration are usually different [[24:212|AFH 10-3]]. Point them to lesson AI.IX.B.
Simulated engine failures done incorrectly have created real emergencies and accidents [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]. A fuel selector or mixture moved for a 'simulated' engine fire is the same trap.
gaps: No source gives a minimum altitude for practicing the emergency descent. The 1,500 ft AGL figures in the AFH are for the steep spiral [[24:212|AFH 10-3]] and for stall recovery [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Choose your own floor with room for the lead and the recovery, and brief it.
Configuration and the emergency descent speed for a given airplane come only from its AFM/POH [[24:82|AFH 3-21]].
No source gives the descent rate a trainer achieves in this configuration, or how much the level-off lead must grow beyond the 10 percent rule at high rates. Measure it with another instructor.
Whether gear or flaps make cabin smoke worse in a particular model, and which vents to use, is model-specific [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]; check the POH.
How long is 'prolonged' practice before the cylinders cool too much is not stated [[24:358|AFH 18-9]]; follow the POH and the engine manufacturer.

activities.title: True or false: the AFH procedure
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: The AFH emergency descent text names VLO among the speeds not to pass.
cards.why: False. It names VNE, VLE and VFE, and VA in turbulence [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]; VLO is defined in chapter 12 [[24:247|AFH 12-16]].

cards.s: Gear speeds may not appear on the airspeed indicator at all.
cards.why: True. They are published in the AFM/POH and usually placarded [[24:247|AFH 12-16]].

cards.s: The AFH puts the propeller in high pitch, low rpm to cut drag in the descent.
cards.why: False. Low pitch, high rpm, so the propeller acts as an aerodynamic brake [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

cards.s: The descent is flown at the maximum allowable airspeed consistent with the procedure used.
cards.why: True. That gives more drag and a high rate of descent [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

cards.s: Unless the manufacturer prohibits it, power goes to idle.
VA is one fixed number at every weight.
cards.why: False. Weight matters; VA may be 100 knots heavy but 90 light [[24:389|AFH G-17]] [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]].

activities.title: Numbers for the brief
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Descending at 2,200 fpm to a specified 3,800 ft. Using the IFH lead, at what altitude do you start the level-off?
items.why: Lead by 10 percent of the descent rate [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]: 0.10 x 2,200 = 220; 3,800 + 220 = 4,020 ft.

items.q: The evaluator gives a target of 135 KIAS. What is the lowest airspeed inside the ACS tolerance?
items.why: +0/-10 knots (CFI ACS AI.XII.A.S5): 135 - 10 = 125 KIAS; anything above 135 is out.

items.q: The specified level-off is 3,800 ft. What is the lowest altitude inside the ACS tolerance?
Your trainer stalls at 52 knots wings level. A level 45 degree bank gives 1.41 G. About what is the stall speed in that bank?
items.why: Stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor, and 45 degrees gives 1.41 [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]: 52 x √1.41 = 52 x 1.187 = 61.7, about 62 knots.

items.q: Same trainer, the bank creeps to 60 degrees in a level turn (2.0 G). About what is the stall speed now?

activities.title: CFI checkride: the evaluator plays your learner
activities.intro: You are the CFI applicant. The evaluator acts as a private pilot learner in a retractable single: gear operating 140 KIAS, gear extended 160 KIAS, flaps extended 110 KIAS, red line 200 KIAS. The POH descent is power idle, propeller forward, gear down, flaps up. Scenario: smoke in the cabin at 7,500 ft.

steps.s: The 'learner' reaches for the flap lever first. What do you say?
options: Fine, flaps first gives the most drag
Stop: on some airplanes flaps can make cabin smoke worse, and the POH descent has them up
Fine, but only to the first notch
Take the controls without a word
steps.why: Gear and/or flaps can aggravate cabin smoke on some airplanes [[24:359|AFH 18-10]], and the configuration must fit the scenario and the POH (CFI ACS AI.XII.A.S2).

steps.s: Configured, the 'learner' rolls left into the descent without looking. Your call?
options: Let it go; the descent is the priority
Stop and clear: look toward the turn and below before rolling in
Let it go, but ask for a radio call
Have them roll right instead
steps.why: Failure to clear for traffic in the turn direction or descent is a listed error [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]; the turn is there to check below [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

steps.s: Gear down, the airspeed reads 166 KIAS. What now?
options: Accept it; 166 is far below the red line
Raise the gear to get rid of the limit
Ease the nose up and check the bank to get under 160; +0 means any overshoot is out
Add power to stabilize the speed
steps.why: With the gear extended, VLE is the limit not to pass [[24:357|AFH 18-8]], and the tolerance is +0 knots (CFI ACS AI.XII.A.S5). Raising the gear at 166 would exceed the gear operating limit [[24:247|AFH 12-16]].

steps.s: Moderate chop begins below 5,000 ft. Which speed rule now applies on top of the others?
options: VA limitations, using any POH turbulence information
VNO only, since the arc is yellow above it
None; the descent speed is fixed by the POH
VFE, because the flaps might be needed
steps.why: In turbulent conditions the pilot also has to comply with VA limitations [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]; many POHs include turbulent air penetration information [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]].

steps.s: Level-off is specified at 4,000 ft. At 2,000 fpm the 'learner' waits until 4,000, then pulls hard while rolling level. Your correction?
options: Fine, the altitude was exactly right
Pull harder next time to stop sooner
Lead by about 200 ft, roll wings level first, then raise the nose gently
Lower the flaps to slow before leveling
steps.why: Lead by 10 percent of the descent rate [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]; a rolling pullout exceeds the design limit more easily, so roll level first and raise the nose gently [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].
